headline: Families read the names as New York marks 25 years

sources.title: 7 moments of silence observed at ground zero
Families honor loved ones 25 years after 9/11 (video, ABC News)

chunks.text: Twenty-five years have {{gone by}} since the attacks of September 11, 2001, in which 2,977 people were killed. On the [[anniversary]], families {{came together}} at the [[memorial plaza]] in New York City for the main [[ceremony]]. The plaza stands on the [[site]] of the [[former]] World Trade Center. Most of the people who died were killed there. The ceremony was not open to the [[general public]]. Only families, [[rescue workers]] and [[invited guests]] were {{let in}}.

verbs.correct: To pass, when talking about time
verbs.wrong: To be forgotten by most people
verbs.why: Ten years can go by before old friends meet again, and a whole afternoon goes by quickly on a long walk. Twenty-five years have gone by since the attacks of September 11, 2001.

verbs.correct: To gather in one place as a group
verbs.wrong: To speak in front of a crowd
verbs.why: Neighbors come together to clean a park after a storm, and a family comes together for a birthday dinner. Families came together at the memorial plaza in New York City on the anniversary.

verbs.correct: To allow someone to enter a place
verbs.wrong: To ask someone to speak first
verbs.why: A guard lets in visitors after checking their tickets, and a parent lets in a child who forgot her key. Only families, rescue workers and invited guests were let in to the ceremony.

chunks.text: Family members {{read out}} the names of the [[victims]] in [[alphabetical order]]. They read [[one at a time]], and each reader {{took over}} from the last. The reading {{went on}} for several hours. When the name of their own [[relative]] {{came up}}, some families added a few words of their own. Every name was said [[aloud]]. For the families, the morning was a time to {{look back on}} the day they lost someone they loved.

verbs.why: A teacher reads out the names on the class list, and a clerk reads out the numbers on a winning ticket. Family members read out the names of the victims in alphabetical order.

verbs.correct: To continue a task from another person
verbs.wrong: To read something silently to yourself
verbs.why: A night nurse takes over from the day nurse at eight, and a second driver takes over halfway through a long trip. At the ceremony, each reader took over from the last.

verbs.correct: To continue for a period of time
verbs.wrong: To be held in a different city
verbs.why: A meeting can go on for two hours, and rain sometimes goes on all night. The reading of the names went on for several hours.

verbs.correct: To be reached in a list or order
verbs.wrong: To be spoken in a very soft voice
verbs.why: When your number comes up at the deli counter, you step to the front, and when a song comes up on the playlist, the screen shows its title. When the name of their own relative came up, some families added a few words.

verbs.correct: To think about a time in the past
verbs.wrong: To take care of someone who is ill
verbs.why: Grandparents look back on their school days with a smile, and a runner looks back on her first race years later. For the families, the morning was a time to look back on the day they lost someone.

chunks.text: Seven [[moments of silence]] marked the morning. The first came at 8:46, the minute the first plane [[struck]] the north tower. At 9:03 the plaza fell quiet a second time, for the moment the second plane struck the south tower. The third, at 9:37, was for the plane that struck the Pentagon. The south tower fell at 9:59. Then came 10:03, when a plane {{came down}} in a field in Shanksville, Pennsylvania. The sixth was for 10:28, when the north tower fell.

verbs.correct: To fall from the air to the ground
verbs.wrong: To fly to a different airport
verbs.why: A kite comes down when the wind stops, and a weather balloon comes down in a field after a long flight. At 10:03, a plane came down in a field in Shanksville, Pennsylvania.

chunks.text: The seventh moment of silence came after the last name was read. It was held for [[survivors]] and rescue workers who have since {{passed away}} from [[illnesses]] linked to the [[toxic dust]] they {{breathed in}}. Ceremonies were also [[held]] at the Pentagon and at the Shanksville site. There, too, people came to remember. For the country, the anniversary was a day to remember a morning that it {{lived through}} twenty-five years ago. The names were read, and the silences were kept.

verbs.why: A friend's grandfather passed away last spring, and a former teacher passed away at ninety after a long life. The seventh silence was for survivors and rescue workers who have since passed away.

verbs.correct: To take air or dust into the lungs
verbs.wrong: To cough without being able to stop
verbs.why: A swimmer breathes in before a long dive, and a runner breathes in deeply at the top of a hill. The seventh silence was for people who became ill from the toxic dust they breathed in.

verbs.correct: To be alive during a hard event
verbs.wrong: To watch an event on television
verbs.why: Some grandparents lived through a war as children, and a coastal town lived through a hurricane last year. The anniversary was a day to remember a morning that the country lived through twenty-five years ago.

mainIdea.s: On the twenty-fifth anniversary of the September 11 attacks, families gathered at the memorial plaza in New York City. They read the names of the victims aloud and kept seven moments of silence.
mainIdea.why: The main ceremony was held on the site of the former World Trade Center, where family members read out every name and the plaza fell quiet seven times.

mainIdea.s: On the twenty-fifth anniversary of the September 11 attacks, families gathered at the memorial plaza in New York City. The ceremony was open to anyone who wished to come and listen to the reading.
mainIdea.why: Close, but the ceremony was not open to the general public; only families, rescue workers and invited guests were let in.

mainIdea.s: On the twenty-fifth anniversary of the September 11 attacks, New York City opened a new museum about that day. Visitors were invited to walk through it for free during the whole of the weekend.
mainIdea.why: No new museum opened; the story is about the ceremony at the memorial plaza, where families read out the names and kept seven moments of silence.
